draft.title: The February Revolution
card: In late February 1917 (March in the Western calendar), bread shortages and cold weather brought crowds onto the streets of Petrograd, the capital. International Women's Day protests on 23 February grew into a general strike within days.
Nicholas II was at the army headquarters, away from the capital. He ordered the troops in Petrograd to restore order by force.
Many soldiers were conscripted peasants and workers who sympathised with the crowds. Some refused to fire, and units of the garrison mutinied and joined the protesters.

Without loyal troops, the tsar had no way to enforce his rule. Leaders of the Duma and his generals urged him to go, and on 2 March (15 March in the Western calendar) Nicholas II abdicated, ending Romanov rule.
draft.remember: The tsar fell when the Petrograd soldiers sided with the strikers, not because of a plan by one party.

a.q: Why did the mutiny of soldiers in Petrograd decide the outcome of the February Revolution?
opts: The tsar could no longer use the army to crush the crowds
The soldiers took over the government on behalf of one party
The soldiers forced the tsar to hand power to the Duma
The mutiny ended the food shortages in the capital
a.why: Autocratic rule depended on force, and once units of the garrison joined the protesters the tsar could not put down the unrest. The soldiers did not set up a government or act for a party: they simply stopped obeying orders to fire.
a.clue: Think about what the tsar needed from the troops.

b.q: Which statement best explains why the February 1917 protests in Petrograd became a revolution, rather than ending like other protests?
opts: Troops sent to stop the crowds joined them instead
A single party organised the strikes from the start
The tsar chose to leave Petrograd and give up power
Food prices fell, so workers demanded political change
b.why: The protests began over bread and grew into a general strike. They became a revolution because soldiers mutinied, which removed the force the tsar relied on. No single party planned the events, and the tsar did not give up power until his position was already lost.
b.clue: Look for what changed between the strikes and the tsar's fall.

a.best: The tsar could no longer use the army to crush the crowds

b.best: Troops sent to stop the crowds joined them instead

problems.detail: The remember line says the fall was 'not because of a plan by one party', but the card never mentions parties or says the events were unplanned. This claim then underpins the wrong options in both questions ('on behalf of one party', 'A single party organised the strikes'). The card should state briefly that no party planned or led the rising.

'Ending Romanov rule' on 2 March simplifies the record. Nicholas abdicated for himself and his son in favour of his brother Michael, and Romanov rule ended only when Michael declined the throne on 3 March.
'Cold weather brought crowds onto the streets' is misleading. The severe winter disrupted food supplies, but accounts usually note that milder weather around 23 February helped bring crowds out.
